title: Everyone gets a place (Joshua 13–19)
hookLine: long lists of borders give every tribe its portion
carry: a place can be a calling

lines: THE BORDER GOES UP, TURNS, GOES DOWN.
cards: The border goes up by a valley. It passes along to a spring of water. It turns toward a mountain, bends around, goes down to the sea.
Then a list of towns, name after name, with their villages. For several chapters the book of Joshua reads like a surveyor's notebook.
But every one of those names was somebody's front door, somebody's well, somebody's field. These chapters are where the wandering ends, and people get an address.

teach.h: GIVEN BY LOT, NAMED BY NAME.
teach.b: The portions are given by lot. Nobody gets to grab the best valley; the land is shared out tribe by tribe, family by family, and each portion is named. Inside the lists there are moments.
Five sisters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, the daughters of Zelophehad, come before Eleazar the priest and Joshua. Their father had no sons.
The Lord commanded Moses, they say, to give us a portion among our brothers. And they receive it, written into the borders with everyone else. A family that could have been left off the map is on it.
Then the tribes of Joseph complain that their share is too small and the hill country too crowded.

teach.h: CLEAR THE FOREST: ROOM IS MADE.
teach.b: Joshua's answer: there's forest up there; clear it, and it's yours. Room can be made. And one tribe gets no territory at all.

Levi, the tribe of the priests and Levites, receives towns to live in among the others, but no portion of land, because, the text says, the Lord, the God of Israel, is their inheritance. Their place is a calling.

teach.h: THE LINES ARE FALLEN IN PLEASANT PLACES.
teach.b: A psalm uses the language of these chapters, lines, lots, portions, like someone looking at their own small share of the world and finding it enough: "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage."

The Hebrew for lines is chavalim, and the book of Joshua uses it when shares fall to the tribe of Manasseh, in the same chapter as the five sisters. A place can be a field, a hillside you clear yourself, or a calling.

how: Jews read the border lists of Joshua 13–19 as part of studying the Former Prophets, and the daughters of Zelophehad, whose claim is told in Numbers and completed in Joshua, are studied as a model of asking for justice.

o: a Levite who received towns instead of land
the tribe that cleared the forest for more room
a man whose five daughters won their own portion

Zelophehad's daughters went without land because they had no brothers
they came to Eleazar and Joshua, reminded them of Moses' command, and received their portion.

games.q: you're one of Zelophehad's daughters. your father died with no sons, and the land is being shared out by family. what do you do?
o: accept that the land will pass you by.
go to the priest and Joshua and claim what Moses promised.
wait until someone thinks of you.
games.why: they stand before Eleazar and Joshua and say: Moses was commanded to give us a portion. and they receive it, among their kin.

practice: Look around at this room, this chair, this small piece of the world that is, for now, yours.
Notice one thing you can see, one thing you can hear, one thing it gives you, and think of the people who share your lines with you, at home, at work, next door.
If you pray, hold the psalm's words: the lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places.

wordCard.voice: Zelophehad, whose five daughters, having no brothers, asked Joshua for a portion of their own, and received it, written into the land alongside everyone else.

orig.note: Hebrew: an inheritance, a portion of land held by a family.
